passages.t: Bildad's last word: how can a man be just before God?
passages.happening:
‘Then Bildad the Shuhite replied’ (verse 1). “Dominion and awe belong to God; He establishes harmony in the heights of heaven. Can His troops be numbered? On whom does His light not rise?” (verses 2-3).

“How then can a man be just before God? How can one born of woman be pure? If even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not pure in His sight, how much less man, who is but a maggot, and the son of man, who is but a worm!” (verses 4-6).
passages.hearers:
This is the shortest speech in the book, and the last time any of the three friends speaks. In the first two rounds all three spoke. In the third, Eliphaz gave a full speech, Bildad gives only these six verses, and Zophar says nothing at all. The friends are running out of arguments. They have described the end of the wicked, called Job to repent and accused him of crimes, and nothing has moved him.

So Bildad falls back on the one point no one disputes: God is great and human beings are small. Job agreed with this long ago (9:2). Bildad's question repeats what Eliphaz said in 4:17-19 and 15:14-16.

The troops of verse 2 are the heavenly hosts that serve God. Many peoples around Israel worshiped the moon and stars as gods. Bildad quietly places them among God's creatures: even they are not pure before him.

Shalom in verse 2, harmony, means order and peace among the powers of heaven. The maggot and the worm were pictures of decay and the grave, and Job has used them of his own body.
passages.later: A psalm says something very different about the same human being: “You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor” (Psalm 8:5). And when Isaiah calls Israel a worm, it is to promise help: “Do not fear, O worm of Jacob, O few men of Israel. I will help you” (Isaiah 41:14).
passages.hard:
Is Bildad right that human beings are nothing but maggots and worms?

His words hold a truth Scripture affirms elsewhere. Human beings are creatures, frail and mortal, and no one can claim to be pure before a holy God on their own merits. Isaiah 41:14 even calls Israel a worm, though in a promise of tender help.

But the Bible's full teaching on humanity is richer than Bildad's. Human beings are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), crowned with glory and honor (Psalm 8:5), and loved by God. Many interpreters note that Bildad uses God's greatness not to comfort Job but to silence him, as if the distance between God and humanity made Job's complaint meaningless. Others observe that his point is not wrong in itself but misapplied, since Job has never claimed to be sinless, only innocent of the friends' charges.

On any reading, Bildad shows how the truth of God's holiness can become a weapon when it is separated from the truth of God's love. No one in distress should be told that they are nothing.
passages.asks: Bildad's last word was that a man is a worm. Ask what you believe about your own worth before God, and where that belief came from. And ask whether you speak to people in pain as creatures God loves or as worms to be silenced.
